concept.title: Extending Coverage with Access Points or Mesh
concept.shortdesc: Use an access point or mesh Wi-Fi system to extend wireless coverage to areas where the main router does not provide a reliable signal.

section.title: Overview
section.p: The provides Wi-Fi coverage within a limited area. Distance, walls, floors, and other physical obstructions can reduce the wireless signal.
If router placement does not provide sufficient coverage, use the or the to extend the wireless network.
section.note: Test the Wi-Fi connection in the required coverage area before you install additional wireless equipment.
Measure signal strength, channel utilization, throughput, latency, and packet loss before you select a coverage-extension method.

section.title: When to Extend Wi-Fi Coverage
section.p: Additional wireless equipment can be necessary in the following conditions:

ul.li: The Wi-Fi signal is weak in frequently used rooms.
Client devices disconnect when users move between areas.
Walls, floors, or large objects reduce the wireless signal.
The home has multiple floors or a large coverage area.
The router cannot be placed near the center of the required coverage area.
Outdoor or detached areas require wireless coverage.
Several devices require a stable connection in an area that is far from the router.

section.note: Check the router location and sources of wireless interference before you add an access point or mesh node. Additional equipment cannot correct all placement or interference problems.

section.title: Wi-Fi Access Point
section.p: The connects to the existing network and provides Wi-Fi coverage in another area.
An access point usually connects to the through Ethernet. The wired connection carries network traffic between the router and the access point.
Use an access point when an Ethernet connection is available in or near the area that requires additional Wi-Fi coverage.
An access point is suitable for the following conditions:

ul.li: The area has an available Ethernet connection.
A stable and consistent backhaul connection is required.
One or more specific areas require additional coverage.
The network requires control over access-point placement and configuration.

section.note: An access point does not replace the router. The access point provides wireless connectivity, and the router continues to manage the home network.
Use a wired backhaul connection when possible. Configure neighbouring access points to reduce channel overlap and excessive coverage overlap.

section.title: Mesh Wi-Fi System
section.p: The uses a main device and one or more mesh nodes to provide Wi-Fi coverage across a larger area.
Mesh nodes communicate with the main router or with other mesh nodes. Together, the devices provide one coordinated wireless network.
Use a mesh system when several areas require additional coverage or when Ethernet cabling is not available.
A mesh system is suitable for the following conditions:

ul.li: Several rooms have a weak Wi-Fi signal.
Users move frequently between different coverage areas.
Ethernet cabling is not available in all required areas.
The network requires centralized management of multiple wireless coverage points.

section.note: A mesh system usually uses the same Wi-Fi network name across all mesh nodes. A compatible client device can remain connected as the user moves through the coverage area.
Roaming decisions can depend on the client device. A client device can remain connected to a distant node even when a nearby node provides a stronger signal.

section.note: Actual performance depends on the network environment, equipment capabilities, backhaul connection, and client devices.

section.title: Select a Coverage Method
section.p: Select the when Ethernet is available and a specific area requires additional wireless coverage.
Select the when multiple areas require coverage or when Ethernet cabling is not available.
Use a wired backhaul for an access point or mesh node when possible. A wired connection does not use wireless capacity to carry traffic between network devices.
section.note: Make sure that the selected access point or mesh system is compatible with the existing network and wireless security configuration.

section.title: Access Point Placement
section.p: Put the in or near the area that requires additional wireless coverage.
Select an open and elevated location. Reduce the number of walls, floors, and large objects between the access point and client devices.
Make sure that the access point has a reliable Ethernet connection to the home network.
section.note: Do not put the access point near heat, water, large metal objects, or equipment that can cause wireless interference.
Provide sufficient coverage overlap to support movement between wireless coverage areas. Avoid excessive overlap that can increase channel utilization and interfere with client roaming.

section.title: Mesh Node Placement
section.p: Put each mesh node between the main router and the area that requires additional coverage.
The mesh node must receive a reliable connection from the main router or another mesh node. Do not put the node in an area where the existing Wi-Fi signal is unusable.
For example, put the in an open area where it can communicate reliably with the and nearby client devices.
section.note: If the mesh system reports a weak connection to the node, move the node closer to the main router or another connected node.
Avoid long chains of wireless mesh nodes. Each wireless hop can affect available capacity, latency, and connection stability.

section.title: Backhaul Connection
section.p: A backhaul connection carries network traffic between the main router and an access point or mesh node.

dlentry.dd: A wired backhaul uses Ethernet to connect the wireless coverage point to the network. This connection can provide consistent performance and does not use Wi-Fi capacity for backhaul traffic.
A wireless backhaul uses Wi-Fi to communicate between mesh devices. Its performance depends on signal strength, interference, distance, and physical obstructions.

section.note: Use a dedicated wireless backhaul band when the supports it. If a dedicated band is not available, client and backhaul traffic can share wireless capacity.

section.title: Network Name and Security
section.p: Use the same security mode across compatible wireless coverage points. In this guide, the wireless security mode is .
A coordinated network can use across the router, access points, and mesh nodes.
section.note: Use the same network name only when all wireless coverage points use compatible security settings. Inconsistent settings can cause connection and roaming problems.
Use consistent SSID, authentication, and encryption settings across roaming coverage areas. Apply a channel plan that reduces interference between neighboring wireless devices.

section.title: Evaluate the Extended Coverage
section.p: Test the Wi-Fi connection after you install an access point or mesh node.
Test the connection near the main router, between coverage points, and in the area that previously had a weak signal.
Check the signal strength, connection stability, and Internet access on more than one client device.
section.note: Move through the required coverage area with a connected smartphone, tablet, or laptop. Confirm that the device remainsconnected.
Record the access point or mesh node, frequency band, channel, signal strength, throughput, latency, and packet loss at each test location. Test roaming behavior between coverage points.

section.title: Coverage Problems
section.p: If the extended network does not provide sufficient coverage, move the access point or mesh node and test the connection again.
If a mesh node has an unstable connection, decrease the distance between the node and the or another connected mesh node.
If the wireless connection is slow, check for interference and review the backhaul connection.
If client devices disconnect while users move between coverage areas, verify that the wireless network names and security settings are consistent.
